projectTitle: Northfield Retail: Investigating a Customer Churn Dashboard Request, Start to Finish
projectTagline: A 22-video, start-to-finish analyst project — SQL, Power BI, Python, Tableau, and Excel, answering one real business question for one fictional retailer.
businessContext:
**Northfield Retail Co.** is a fictional mid-size specialty retailer. Their Sales Director walks into your office and says: "We're losing customers and I don't know why. Build me a dashboard." That sentence is the entire brief you're given — no agreed definition of a lost customer, no agreed metric, no agreed audience.

This series follows one analyst project from that single vague sentence through to a finished, trusted dashboard and a presentation that tells the Sales Director something she didn't already know — using exactly the tools taught earlier in this path: T-SQL, Power BI, a little Python, Tableau, and Excel.
architectureSummary: By the end of this series you'll have: a T-SQL query that defines, precisely, what counts as an active versus a churned customer; a Power BI dashboard with an executive summary page and a region/segment drill-down; a small Python script that flags statistical outliers Power BI's visuals miss; a Tableau version of the same core view for the field team that already lives in Tableau; and an Excel-based reconciliation you ran before anyone else saw the numbers, to make sure they were right before they were trusted.

lessons.title: Meeting the Sales Director: What "Are We Losing Customers?" Actually Means
lessons.summary: Turning a one-sentence, undefined request into a specific, answerable analytical question.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Over the next 22 videos, you'll answer one real business question for a fictional specialty retailer, **Northfield Retail Co.**: "Are we losing customers, and why?" You'll build a T-SQL query that defines what that question even means in data, a Power BI dashboard with an executive and a drill-down view, a small Python check Power BI can't do on its own, a Tableau version for a field team that already works in Tableau, and an Excel reconciliation that catches a mistake before anyone else sees it.

This video is the one meeting that decides whether everything after it is useful or wasted effort.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine your boss walks up and says, "I think we're losing customers, go make me a chart." That sounds simple, but it's actually a trick question — losing customers compared to when? What counts as "lost"? Someone who hasn't bought anything in a month? Six months? A year?

Your job in this video is to sit down with your boss and turn that one confusing sentence into a clear, specific question you can actually answer with data — before you open a single tool.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This lesson is about the gap between a stated problem and an analyzable one. "We're losing customers" is not a metric — it has no defined denominator, no time window, and no agreed-upon churn definition. Different reasonable definitions of churn (90 days inactive versus 180, versus a declared cancellation) can produce wildly different churn rates from the exact same transaction table, and if you pick one without agreement, you will be the one blamed when finance's number doesn't match yours.

Your job here is to leave the meeting with an operational definition precise enough that two different analysts, given the same data, would compute the same number.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Don't open SQL yet. Ask these questions first

- What does "losing a customer" mean, operationally? No purchase in X days? An explicit cancellation?
- Compared to what — last quarter? Last year? A rolling average?
- Is this about all customers, or a specific segment (new vs. returning, a particular region)?
- Who's the audience for this — just you, or will this go to the CFO?
- Is this a one-time analysis, or does it need to refresh on a schedule?

## Step 2 — Run the actual conversation

```
Q: When you say "losing customers," what made you say that?
A: Repeat sales in the Southeast region feel lower than they used to. I don't have hard numbers, just a feeling from talking to the regional managers.

Q: What would make you comfortable saying "yes, we have a churn problem" versus "no, it's normal fluctuation"?
A: I guess... if a meaningful number of customers who used to buy regularly just stopped, for no obvious reason like a store closing.

Q: How should we define "stopped buying"? No purchase in 90 days? 180?
A: I don't know — what's normal for a specialty retailer?

Q: Is this just the Southeast, or all regions?
A: Start with all regions so we have a baseline, then I want to see the Southeast specifically.

Q: Who else will see this?
A: Just me for now. If the number's bad, I'll take it to the CFO myself.
```

Notice the Sales Director doesn't actually know the right churn window — that's not a gap in her knowledge you should quietly fill in on your own. It's a decision to make together, informed by what's reasonable for this kind of business, and to write down.

## Step 3 — Propose a specific, defensible definition and get it agreed

```
NORTHFIELD RETAIL — CHURN ANALYSIS, WORKING DEFINITION

Active customer:      At least one purchase in the trailing 90 days
Churned customer:      No purchase in 90+ days, but had purchased at least
                       twice in the prior 12 months (excludes true one-time
                       buyers, who were never "retained" in the first place)
Baseline scope:        All regions, trailing 12 months
Follow-up scope:       Southeast region specifically, same definition
Audience:              Sales Director only, for now
Cadence:               One-time analysis, not yet a recurring report
```

## Step 4 — Confirm it in writing, then move on

Send this definition back before building anything: "Here's exactly how I'm going to calculate this — does this match what you're picturing, or does the 90-day window feel wrong to you?" This single email is what prevents the single worst outcome in analytics: building a technically correct dashboard that answers a question nobody actually asked.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Had the intake with the Sales Director. Operational definition: active = purchase in trailing 90 days, churned = no purchase in 90+ days but 2+ purchases in the prior 12 months, so we exclude true one-time buyers. Baseline is all regions trailing 12 months, with a Southeast-specific follow-up. One-time analysis for now, audience is just her. I'll have the T-SQL query defining this drafted next.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Met with the Sales Director. She had a feeling the Southeast region is losing repeat customers but no hard numbers. We agreed on a specific definition of what counts as a lost customer and confirmed it in writing before starting any build — that's the step that keeps this from turning into a dashboard nobody trusts. Baseline analysis covers all regions first, then a Southeast deep-dive.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The Sales Director had a hunch, not a number. Before building anything, we pinned down exactly what "losing customers" means in a way everyone agrees on — that's the step most teams skip, and it's usually why a finished dashboard gets challenged later. We're building against an agreed, written-down definition from day one.

lessons.title: Turning "Build Me a Dashboard" Into a Specific Question
lessons.summary: Generalizing the intake pattern from lesson 1 into a repeatable habit for the next vague request.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Lesson 1 was one conversation about one request. This lesson is where that conversation turns into a habit you can run on literally any vague ask, for the rest of your career, not just this project. Before you touch SQL in the next phase, you need a checklist you can run in five minutes the next time someone says "just give me a number" or "can you pull a report on this."

We're building the reusable version of what just happened with the Sales Director: a short, repeatable intake routine, so the next vague request doesn't require you to reinvent the conversation from scratch.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about a doctor. A good doctor doesn't just hear "my stomach hurts" and immediately hand you medicine. They ask: where exactly does it hurt, since when, does anything make it better or worse, have you eaten anything weird? Only after those questions do they know what to actually do.

This lesson turns the conversation from the last video into that same kind of checklist — a short list of questions you ask yourself, every single time, before you start building anything, no matter who's asking or what they're asking for.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Requirements intake isn't a one-time skill you used once on the Sales Director — it's a discipline, and like any discipline it only holds up if it's repeatable under time pressure, when a VP is standing over your shoulder and "just five minutes" feels tempting. The five questions that mattered in lesson 1 generalize cleanly: what's the metric (and is it actually defined), what's it being compared against, what's the scope (population, time window, segment), who's the audience, and what's the cadence (one-time vs. recurring).

The reason this matters professionally is that skipping intake doesn't save time — it moves the time cost downstream, to rework, and adds a trust cost on top of it, because the second version looks like you didn't know what you were doing the first time.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Write down the five questions as a standing checklist

```
THE FIVE-QUESTION INTAKE CHECKLIST

1. METRIC      — What exact number or definition are we talking about?
                 Has anyone defined it in writing before, and does that
                 definition still apply?
2. COMPARISON   — Compared to what? A prior period, a target, another
                 segment, or just "is this normal"?
3. SCOPE        — What population, time window, and segment? All
                 customers or one region? This month or trailing 12?
4. AUDIENCE     — Who actually reads this, and what decision will they
                 make from it?
5. CADENCE      — One-time analysis, or does this need to refresh on a
                 schedule going forward?
```

This is the same five things you implicitly asked the Sales Director in lesson 1 — now it's explicit, so you don't have to improvise it under pressure next time.

## Step 2 — Test it on a different, smaller request

Suppose a merchandising manager stops by next month and says, "Can you tell me our best sellers?" Run the checklist silently in your head before answering:

```
Metric:      "Best seller" by units sold, or by revenue, or by margin?
             Those three can produce three different top-10 lists.
Comparison:  Best sellers this month, or best sellers all-time?
Scope:       All stores, or the stores she manages specifically?
Audience:    Just her, or is this going into a buying-committee deck?
Cadence:     One-time look, or a report she wants every Monday?
```

Notice you didn't need a new framework for a completely different request — the same five questions did the job.

## Step 3 — Know the red flags that mean you're not ready to build

If you catch yourself thinking any of the following, stop and go back to the checklist:

- "I'll just guess the time window and adjust later if they complain."
- "They didn't say who else would see it, so I'll assume just them."
- "It's probably a one-time thing."

Each of those is an unanswered question wearing a guess as a disguise, and it's exactly how the Sales Director's dashboard would have turned into a 4% churn number that nobody agreed to trust, if lesson 1 had skipped the conversation.

## Step 4 — Send the same kind of confirmation email every time

```
Hi [name] — before I start building, here's exactly how I'm reading your
request: [metric], compared to [comparison], for [scope], going to
[audience], as a [one-time / recurring] analysis. Let me know if any of
that doesn't match what you had in mind.
```

This email takes two minutes to write and costs you nothing if the answer is "yes, exactly." It's genuinely cheap insurance against the expensive version of this mistake.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Codifying the intake conversation from the Sales Director meeting into a standing five-question checklist (metric, comparison, scope, audience, cadence) so future requests get the same discipline without re-deriving it each time. Nothing changes about the Northfield churn project itself — this is the reusable process artifact that came out of doing it once correctly.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We now have a written five-minute intake step that runs before any build starts, on this project or the next one. It doesn't add meaningful time to the schedule, but it does mean a confirmation email goes out before work begins — so if a stakeholder's expectations shift, we catch it on day one instead of at delivery.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We turned one good intake conversation into a repeatable habit, so the next vague request gets the same five-minute check instead of a guess. That's the cheapest insurance against building the wrong thing well.

lessons.title: Deciding What Counts as a Churned Customer
lessons.summary: Stress-testing the churn definition against edge cases before it gets baked into SQL.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: The Sales Director agreed to a definition in lesson 1: active means a purchase in the trailing 90 days, churned means no purchase in 90+ days but at least two purchases in the prior 12 months. That definition sounds settled, but it hasn't been tested against real customer behavior yet. In this lesson, before any SQL gets written, we run the definition against the actual messy cases that show up in a specialty retailer's data — and tighten it into something you can defend.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine deciding when a cactus counts as "dead." If you check on it every week, it might look the same for months and then suddenly bloom once a year. If your rule is "no new growth in 90 days means it's dead," you'd wrongly declare a perfectly healthy cactus dead every single year, right before it blooms.

Customers can be like that too — some genuinely only shop once a year, like around the holidays, and they're not "lost," they're just dormant on a schedule. This lesson is about catching cases like that before they get mislabeled.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A churn rule that looks clean in a working-definition document can still misclassify real customers once it meets actual transaction data. The specific risks here are false positives: legitimately low-frequency but loyal customers (holiday-only shoppers, for instance) who will cycle in and out of "churned" status every year under a flat 90-day rule, and ambiguous events like returns that shouldn't count as evidence of continued engagement the way a genuine purchase does.

The fix isn't to throw out the agreed definition from lesson 1 — it's to add scoped exceptions that make the definition more precise without changing what it fundamentally measures, and to get those exceptions approved the same way the original definition was.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Profile the data for edge cases before writing the final query

Run a quick diagnostic query to see what you're dealing with:

```sql
SELECT
    CASE
        WHEN PurchaseCount12Mo = 0 THEN '0 purchases, prior 12mo'
        WHEN PurchaseCount12Mo = 1 THEN 'exactly 1 purchase, prior 12mo'
        WHEN PurchaseCount12Mo >= 2 THEN '2+ purchases, prior 12mo'
    END AS PurchaseBucket,
    COUNT(*) AS CustomerCount
FROM (
    SELECT CustomerID, COUNT(*) AS PurchaseCount12Mo
    FROM Sales.Orders
    WHERE OrderDate >= DATEADD(MONTH, -12, @AsOfDate)
      AND OrderDate < @AsOfDate
      AND OrderTotal > 0
    GROUP BY CustomerID
) AS PurchaseCounts
GROUP BY CASE
    WHEN PurchaseCount12Mo = 0 THEN '0 purchases, prior 12mo'
    WHEN PurchaseCount12Mo = 1 THEN 'exactly 1 purchase, prior 12mo'
    WHEN PurchaseCount12Mo >= 2 THEN '2+ purchases, prior 12mo'
END;
```

This surfaces three real edge cases worth deciding on before locking the definition.

## Step 2 — Decide and document each edge case

```
ADDENDUM TO THE WORKING CHURN DEFINITION (lesson 1)

Edge case 1 — One-time buyers
  Ruling: Unchanged from the original definition. A customer with only
  one purchase ever was never retained, so they can't "churn." They are
  excluded from both the active and churned counts and reported
  separately as "never retained."

Edge case 2 — Returns and refunds
  Ruling: A return or refund with a net OrderTotal of zero or less does
  NOT count as a purchase for recency purposes. Only a completed sale
  with a positive net amount resets the "last purchase" clock. Otherwise
  a customer could look "active" purely by returning something.

Edge case 3 — Seasonal / holiday-only shoppers
  Ruling: Customers with 2+ purchases in the prior 12 months, where every
  purchase falls inside a single recurring 6-week window (e.g. late
  November through early January) in each of the last two years, are
  flagged separately as "Seasonal" rather than counted in the primary
  churned total. They still appear on the drill-down page, just in their
  own category, so the headline number isn't inflated by customers who
  are behaving exactly as expected.

Edge case 4 — Wholesale / B2B accounts
  Ruling: Out of scope. This analysis is about retail/consumer churn.
  Accounts flagged Segment = 'Wholesale' are excluded entirely from both
  the active and churned counts.
```

## Step 3 — Confirm the addendum, don't just assume it

Send a short follow-up, the same way as lesson 1: "Quick addition to the definition we agreed on — I found a few edge cases in the data (holiday-only shoppers, returns, wholesale accounts) and here's how I'm planning to handle each one so they don't distort the number. Flag anything that looks wrong before I build the query." This is a five-minute email that prevents a much longer argument after the dashboard ships.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Added an addendum to the churn definition: returns/refunds (OrderTotal <= 0) don't count as a qualifying purchase for recency, Segment = 'Wholesale' accounts are excluded from the population entirely, and customers with 2+ purchases confined to the same recurring 6-week seasonal window in each of the last two years get broken out as 'Seasonal' rather than folded into the primary churned count. None of this changes the core 90-day/12-month definition, it just scopes it correctly.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Before locking the query logic, we ran the agreed definition against real data and found a few edge cases — returns, wholesale accounts, holiday-only shoppers — that needed explicit rulings so the number doesn't get challenged later. Added one short confirmation round-trip with the Sales Director; no change to the overall timeline.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We stress-tested the definition against real customer behavior before building anything, and found a few cases — like holiday-only shoppers — that needed a specific rule so they don't get wrongly counted as lost customers every single year. Small catch now, avoided a credibility problem later.

lessons.title: Choosing Power BI vs. Tableau vs. Excel for Each Audience
lessons.summary: Matching each deliverable to the tool its actual audience already trusts and uses.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: This project is about to produce the same core finding in three different tools: Power BI, Tableau, and Excel. That's not indecision and it's not busywork — each tool is going to a different audience who already trusts it. In this lesson we decide, on paper, which tool serves which audience and why, before building any of them.
lessons.explainSimple: If you had important news for your grandmother and your little cousin, you wouldn't explain it the exact same way to both of them — you'd use the words each one already understands. Power BI, Tableau, and Excel are like that. Different people at Northfield are already comfortable with different tools, so instead of forcing everyone to learn a new one, we deliver the same true answer in whichever tool each audience already speaks.
lessons.explainProfessional: Tool choice should follow the audience and the delivery mechanism, not personal preference or whichever tool is newest. Northfield's leadership already lives in Power BI with org-wide licensing and a refresh/governance pattern in place, so that's the system of record for the executive view. The field/regional team already works in Tableau day-to-day, so a second build there isn't redundant — it's meeting people where they are instead of asking a regional manager to learn a new BI tool just to see numbers about their own stores. Excel plays a third, different role entirely: it's not a deliverable, it's the analyst's own independent reconciliation tool, used precisely because it doesn't depend on the same Power Query/DAX engine that produced the numbers you're trying to verify.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Inventory who actually needs to see this and what they already use

```
Audience                 Currently lives in         Needs refresh?
-----------------------  --------------------------  ---------------
Sales Director / exec    Power BI (org standard)     Yes, ongoing
Regional/field managers   Tableau (existing team tool) Yes, ongoing
You (the analyst)         Excel                       No, one-time QA
```

## Step 2 — Write the decision, with reasons, not just the tool names

```
DECISION LOG

Power BI  — Executive summary + drill-down. Reason: this is where
            leadership already looks for company metrics; it supports
            scheduled refresh against SQL Server without extra licensing.

Tableau   — Same core churn view, rebuilt for the regional/field team.
            Reason: they already use Tableau for store-level reporting;
            forcing them into Power BI would hurt adoption more than any
            feature difference between the two tools would help.

Excel     — Independent reconciliation only. Reason: it is deliberately
            NOT the same engine as Power BI's Power Query/DAX, so it is a
            genuine second opinion, not a restatement of the same
            calculation. It will not be shared outside the analyst.
```

## Step 3 — Protect a single source of truth for the logic itself

All three tools will consume the same T-SQL definition of active/churned from lesson 7 — the SQL does the business-logic heavy lifting once, and Power BI, Tableau, and Excel each just present that same answer differently. The goal is one definition, three presentations — never three independently-invented definitions that happen to look similar.

## Step 4 — Set expectations about what each tool is NOT

Excel is not getting published anywhere. Tableau is not replacing Power BI as the executive view. Power BI is not going to the field team as their daily tool. Writing this down up front avoids someone later asking "why isn't this in Tableau too" about a deliverable that was never meant to be.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Decided the shared T-SQL query is the single source of truth for the active/churned logic; Power BI and Tableau each consume it independently for their respective audiences, and Excel is a standalone reconciliation check using different formulas against the same raw tables, not the same engine. No business logic gets reimplemented three separate times — only the presentation layer differs.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Scoped the deliverables: a Power BI report for the Sales Director/leadership, a Tableau rebuild for the regional field team who already work in that tool, and an Excel check that stays internal to the analysis and isn't a shipped deliverable. This confirms three builds, not one, before timeline estimates go out.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We're not duplicating effort — we're meeting each audience in the tool they already trust, so leadership sees it in Power BI and the field team sees it in Tableau, without anyone needing to learn a new tool to understand the same finding.

lessons.title: Planning the SQL Query Before Opening Power BI
lessons.summary: Sketching the query logic on paper so the dashboard build doesn't start from a shaky foundation.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: Before opening SQL Server Management Studio, we're sketching the query's logic on paper: what tables it needs, what the output grain is, and the plain-English version of the active/churned classification. This is the bridge between the agreed definition from lessons 1 and 3 and the actual T-SQL in lesson 7.
lessons.explainSimple: Before you cook anything, a good cook reads the whole recipe once, lays out the ingredients, and pictures the steps in order. If you just start throwing things in a pan, you find out halfway through that you needed an ingredient you don't have. Planning the query on paper first means you find the gaps in your plan with a pencil, which is a lot cheaper than finding them halfway through writing SQL.
lessons.explainProfessional: The two decisions that matter most before writing a single line of SQL are the grain of the output (exactly one row per customer, not one row per order) and the reference point for "today" (a single parameterized as-of date, not a hardcoded GETDATE() buried inside the logic). Getting the grain wrong means joins will fan out and silently inflate counts — which is exactly the kind of bug lesson 17 digs into later. Parameterizing the as-of date means the same query can be re-run against any historical date for testing, which matters because you can't validate a churn classification against a moving target.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — List the source tables and the fields you actually need

```
Sales.Orders     (CustomerID, OrderDate, OrderTotal, StoreID)
Sales.Customers  (CustomerID, Region, Segment, LoyaltyTier, SignupDate)
Sales.Stores     (StoreID, Region, StoreName)
```

## Step 2 — Fix the output grain before anything else

The query must return exactly one row per CustomerID, with a status column. Every join and aggregation downstream has to preserve that grain — if a join against Orders or Stores can produce more than one matching row per customer, something will need to be pre-aggregated first (like last purchase date) rather than joined directly.

## Step 3 — Write the logic in plain English before SQL

```
For each customer:
  last_order_date  = the most recent OrderDate with OrderTotal > 0
  days_since_last   = days between last_order_date and @AsOfDate
  purchases_12mo    = count of orders with OrderTotal > 0 in the
                      12 months immediately before @AsOfDate

  if days_since_last <= 90:                  status = 'Active'
  else if days_since_last > 90
       and purchases_12mo >= 2:              status = 'Churned'
  else:                                      status = 'Not Yet Retained'
```

This is a direct translation of the lesson 1 and lesson 3 rulings — nothing new is being decided here, just restated as logic.

## Step 4 — Parameterize "today"

Use a single declared variable, `@AsOfDate`, instead of `GETDATE()` scattered through the query. That one change means you can re-run the exact same query against last month's data to sanity-check the trend, which you'll need for the executive summary page in lesson 10.

## Step 5 — Write down what this query will NOT do

This query produces raw classification, not a rate, not a trend, and not a region breakdown with percentages — those are DAX measures (lesson 9) and Tableau calculated fields (lesson 13) built on top of this output. Keeping the SQL focused on classification only keeps it simple enough to verify by hand.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Locked the output grain at one row per CustomerID and decided to parameterize the reference date as @AsOfDate rather than GETDATE(), specifically so the query is re-runnable against historical dates for validation. Logic translated to plain-English pseudocode first, matching the lesson 1/3 definition exactly, before any SQL syntax gets written.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: This is a short planning step — about half a day — that happens before the actual query gets written, and it's the reason the SQL build in the next phase should go quickly without major rework.
workplaceExplanation.executive: No change visible yet — this is the planning step that keeps the technical build on schedule, by working out the logic on paper instead of discovering problems midway through coding it.

lessons.title: Sketching the Dashboard Layout on Paper First
lessons.summary: Wireframing the executive summary and drill-down pages before touching Power BI Desktop.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: We're wireframing the two Power BI pages — an executive summary and a region/segment drill-down — on paper before opening Power BI Desktop, so the build in lessons 10 and 11 is just filling in a known shape rather than designing while building.
lessons.explainSimple: Before you build a treehouse, you sketch it first — where the ladder goes, how big the floor is, where the roof is. If you just start nailing boards together, you end up redoing a lot of it. A dashboard is the same: draw the boxes and where the numbers go before you touch the software.
lessons.explainProfessional: The guiding principle here is the inverted pyramid: put the headline conclusion where it's seen first, with supporting detail available but not forced on the reader. The Sales Director needs to get the churn rate and the direction of the trend in about five seconds without being told what to look at — that's the executive summary page. The drill-down page exists for the second question she already told us was coming in lesson 1: the Southeast-specific follow-up. Designing both pages before opening Power BI avoids the common failure mode of a dashboard that grows one visual at a time until it becomes a junk drawer nobody can read quickly.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Sketch the executive summary page layout

```
+----------------------------------------------------------+
|  NORTHFIELD RETAIL — CUSTOMER CHURN, ALL REGIONS           |
+------------------+------------------+----------------------+
|  ACTIVE CUSTOMERS |  CHURNED        |  CHURN RATE          |
|      38,500-ish   |   ~1,580        |      4.1%            |
+------------------+------------------+----------------------+
|      [ trailing 12-month trend line of churn rate ]        |
+----------------------------------------------------------+
|  One-sentence callout: "Churn is concentrated in the       |
|   Southeast region — see drill-down."                      |
+----------------------------------------------------------+
```

Three KPI cards, one trend line, one plain-language callout. Nothing else on this page.

## Step 2 — Sketch the drill-down page layout

```
+----------------------------------------------------------+
|  CHURN BY REGION AND SEGMENT                               |
+----------------------------------------------------------+
|  [ bar chart: churn rate by region, Southeast highlighted ]|
+----------------------------------------------------------+
|  [ matrix: Region x Segment, churn rate + customer counts ]|
+----------------------------------------------------------+
|  Slicers: Region, Segment, Loyalty Tier                    |
+----------------------------------------------------------+
```

## Step 3 — Run the five-second test on the sketch, not the software

Cover the sketch and ask: if the Sales Director saw only the top third of this page for five seconds, would she know whether there's a problem and roughly how big it is? If the answer isn't an obvious yes, the layout needs to change before anything gets built, not after.

## Step 4 — Decide what's deliberately left off page one

Segment breakdowns, loyalty tier detail, and store-level detail are all real and useful — but they go on the drill-down page, not the summary. The executive page's job is the headline; a reader who wants more has a second page to go to on purpose.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Wireframed two pages before opening Power BI: an exec summary (3 KPI cards, one trend line, one callout) and a drill-down (region/segment matrix, bar chart, slicers). This gives a fixed visual spec to build against in lessons 10-11 instead of designing live.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Confirmed the report will be exactly two pages with a defined set of visuals on each, agreed before build time is spent — this is what the Power BI build in the next few lessons is actually implementing.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The dashboard is being built so you can get the headline in about five seconds, with more detail only one click away if you want it — not a page you have to study.

lessons.title: Writing the T-SQL Query That Defines "Active Customer"
lessons.summary: Translating the agreed churn definition into an exact, testable SQL query.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: This is where the agreed definition from lessons 1 and 3 becomes real, testable T-SQL: one query against Northfield's SQL Server database that returns exactly one row per customer, with a status of Active, Churned, or Not Yet Retained, built on a single parameterized as-of date.
lessons.explainSimple: Remember the plain-English rule from the last lesson — "active if they bought something in the last 90 days, churned if they didn't but used to shop regularly"? This lesson just translates that sentence into the language a database actually understands, one careful piece at a time, so the computer can sort every single customer into the right bucket automatically.
lessons.explainProfessional: This query uses two CTEs feeding a final SELECT: one resolving the last qualifying purchase date per customer, one resolving the prior-12-month purchase count per customer, joined back to the customer dimension so customers with zero orders still appear (hence the LEFT JOINs). The classification itself is a CASE expression that mirrors the lesson 3 addendum exactly — OrderTotal > 0 filters out returns/refunds, and the Wholesale segment exclusion happens in the base customer filter. Declaring @AsOfDate as a variable rather than calling GETDATE() inline is what makes this testable against historical snapshots.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Declare the as-of date as a variable

```sql
DECLARE @AsOfDate DATE = '2026-09-30';  -- swap for GETDATE() in production
```

## Step 2 — Build the last-qualifying-purchase CTE

```sql
WITH LastPurchase AS (
    SELECT
        CustomerID,
        MAX(OrderDate) AS LastOrderDate
    FROM Sales.Orders
    WHERE OrderTotal > 0          -- excludes returns/refunds per lesson 3
    GROUP BY CustomerID
),
```

## Step 3 — Build the trailing-12-month purchase count CTE

```sql
PriorYearPurchaseCount AS (
    SELECT
        CustomerID,
        COUNT(*) AS PurchaseCount12Mo
    FROM Sales.Orders
    WHERE OrderTotal > 0
      AND OrderDate >= DATEADD(MONTH, -12, @AsOfDate)
      AND OrderDate <  @AsOfDate
    GROUP BY CustomerID
)
```

## Step 4 — Join back to the customer dimension and classify

```sql
SELECT
    c.CustomerID,
    c.Region,
    c.Segment,
    lp.LastOrderDate,
    DATEDIFF(DAY, lp.LastOrderDate, @AsOfDate)     AS DaysSinceLastOrder,
    ISNULL(py.PurchaseCount12Mo, 0)                AS PurchaseCount12Mo,
    CASE
        WHEN lp.LastOrderDate IS NULL THEN 'Never Purchased'
        WHEN DATEDIFF(DAY, lp.LastOrderDate, @AsOfDate) <= 90
            THEN 'Active'
        WHEN DATEDIFF(DAY, lp.LastOrderDate, @AsOfDate) > 90
             AND ISNULL(py.PurchaseCount12Mo, 0) >= 2
            THEN 'Churned'
        ELSE 'Not Yet Retained'
    END AS CustomerStatus
FROM Sales.Customers c
LEFT JOIN LastPurchase lp
    ON lp.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
LEFT JOIN PriorYearPurchaseCount py
    ON py.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
WHERE c.Segment <> 'Wholesale';   -- out of scope per lesson 3
```

## Step 5 — Sanity-check the result before trusting it

```sql
SELECT CustomerStatus, COUNT(*) AS Customers
FROM (/* the query above */) AS Classified
GROUP BY CustomerStatus
ORDER BY Customers DESC;
```

For the baseline run, this should land close to: Active a large majority, Churned around 1,580 customers, with the rest split between Never Purchased and Not Yet Retained. If the Churned count comes back at zero or at nearly the entire customer base, the date math or the filter logic has a bug — don't move on to Power BI until the distribution looks plausible.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Query is two CTEs (last qualifying purchase date, trailing-12-month purchase count) joined back to Customers with LEFT JOINs so zero-order customers still appear, classified with a CASE expression matching the lesson 1/3 definition exactly, driven off a single @AsOfDate variable for testability. Returns are excluded via OrderTotal > 0 and Wholesale is filtered in the base WHERE clause.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The core SQL query is done and sanity-checked against the agreed definition. This is the foundation every other tool (Power BI, Tableau, Excel) will build on top of, so getting it right here protects the rest of the schedule.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The query that defines who counts as an active versus a lost customer is written and checked against the numbers we'd expect to see — this is the foundation everything else in the dashboard sits on.

lessons.title: Pulling the Data Into Power BI and Shaping It
lessons.summary: Importing the query results and shaping them into a usable model.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: Now we bring the SQL query's output into Power BI Desktop and shape it into a model that DAX measures can actually use cleanly — a proper Date dimension table, correct data types, and relationships, instead of one flat imported table.
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine you just got a big box of LEGO bricks sorted into one giant pile. Before you can build anything cool, you sort them by color and size so you can grab what you need quickly. Shaping data in Power BI is the same idea — organizing the raw information into neat, connected tables so later steps (the formulas, the charts) are easy instead of messy.
lessons.explainProfessional: Importing the lesson 7 query directly gets you a flat table, but a flat table makes time intelligence awkward and invites ad-hoc date logic scattered across measures instead of one Date dimension everything relates to. The model needs a proper Date table (marked as a date table) related to Orders on OrderDate, a Customers dimension related one-to-many to Orders on CustomerID, and correct data types set at the Power Query step rather than left to auto-detection, since auto-detected types are a common source of silent DAX errors later.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Connect and import

Get Data → SQL Server → point at the Northfield database → import `Sales.Orders`, `Sales.Customers`, and `Sales.Stores` as separate tables (not just the lesson 7 classification query — the model needs the raw fact and dimension tables so DAX measures can do their own time intelligence, not just inherit one hardcoded as-of date).

## Step 2 — Shape each table in Power Query Editor

- **Sales.Orders**: set `OrderDate` to Date type, `OrderTotal` to Fixed Decimal, filter out rows where `OrderTotal <= 0` is NOT desired here — keep returns visible in the fact table itself; the exclusion belongs in the DAX measures (lesson 9), not baked into the import, so other analyses can still see returns if needed.
- **Sales.Customers**: set `Region` and `Segment` to Text, remove any Wholesale-only columns you don't need, keep `SignupDate` as Date type.
- Rename ambiguous column names (e.g. `ID` → `CustomerID`) so relationships are unambiguous later.

## Step 3 — Build a proper Date dimension

Don't rely on Power BI's auto date/time. Add a calculated table:

```dax
'Date' =
CALENDAR ( DATE ( 2023, 1, 1 ), DATE ( 2026, 12, 31 ) )
```

Then add Year, Month, and MonthName columns off of it, and mark it as the official Date table (Table tools → Mark as Date Table, using the `Date` column).

## Step 4 — Build the relationships

```
Sales.Orders[OrderDate]   -- many  -->  'Date'[Date]            -- one
Sales.Orders[CustomerID]  -- many  -->  Sales.Customers[CustomerID] -- one
Sales.Orders[StoreID]     -- many  -->  Sales.Stores[StoreID]      -- one
```

All relationships should be single-direction (one-to-many) unless there's a specific reason for bidirectional filtering — bidirectional relationships are exactly the kind of thing that causes the double-counting bug diagnosed in lesson 17, so don't add them by default.

## Step 5 — Disable Power BI's automatic date hierarchies

File → Options → Current File → Data Load → uncheck "Auto Date/Time." This forces every date-based visual and measure to use the real `'Date'` table instead of a hidden auto-generated one per column, which keeps the model's behavior predictable.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Modeled this as a star schema: Orders as the fact table, Customers and Stores as dimensions, plus a dedicated calculated Date table marked as the official date table, all single-direction relationships. Disabled auto date/time so there's exactly one date hierarchy in the model, not a hidden one per table.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Data is imported and shaped into a proper model — this step took about a day and sets up everything downstream (the DAX measures, both report pages) to work correctly without rework later.
workplaceExplanation.executive: No visible change yet — this is the behind-the-scenes organizing step that makes the actual dashboard, coming in the next couple of lessons, fast and reliable.

lessons.title: Building the DAX Measures for Churn Rate
lessons.summary: Turning the written churn definition into DAX that matches it exactly.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: With the model shaped in lesson 8, we now write the DAX measures that reproduce the lesson 7 SQL logic inside Power BI itself — Active Customers, Churned Customers, and Churn Rate — so they respond correctly to slicers on Region, Segment, and date range instead of being frozen at one fixed as-of date.
lessons.explainSimple: The SQL query gave us one fixed snapshot, like a single photograph. DAX measures are more like a smart camera that can retake that photograph instantly for whatever you point it at — all regions, just the Southeast, just last month — without you having to go back and rewrite the question each time.
lessons.explainProfessional: The key design choice is computing the "as of" reference date from the model itself — MAX of the Date table, respecting whatever filter context is active — rather than hardcoding a date, so the measures stay correct as new data refreshes in. Active Customers is a straightforward DISTINCTCOUNT inside a 90-day CALCULATE window. Churned Customers has to independently verify both the inactivity condition and the prior-engagement condition per customer using FILTER over VALUES, since DAX has no direct equivalent of SQL's CASE-over-aggregated-CTEs — it has to be rebuilt as row-by-row logic evaluated in context.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — A reusable "as of" date measure

```dax
As Of Date =
MAX ( 'Date'[Date] )
```

## Step 2 — Active Customers

```dax
Active Customers =
VAR AsOf = [As Of Date]
RETURN
CALCULATE (
    DISTINCTCOUNT ( Sales_Orders[CustomerID] ),
    Sales_Orders[OrderTotal] > 0,
    DATESBETWEEN ( 'Date'[Date], AsOf - 90, AsOf )
)
```

## Step 3 — Churned Customers

```dax
Churned Customers =
VAR AsOf = [As Of Date]
RETURN
COUNTROWS (
    FILTER (
        VALUES ( Sales_Customers[CustomerID] ),
        VAR LastOrder =
            CALCULATE ( MAX ( Sales_Orders[OrderDate] ), Sales_Orders[OrderTotal] > 0 )
        VAR DaysSince = DATEDIFF ( LastOrder, AsOf, DAY )
        VAR PriorYearPurchases =
            CALCULATE (
                COUNTROWS ( Sales_Orders ),
                Sales_Orders[OrderTotal] > 0,
                DATESBETWEEN ( 'Date'[Date], AsOf - 365, AsOf )
            )
        RETURN
            NOT ISBLANK ( LastOrder )
                && DaysSince > 90
                && PriorYearPurchases >= 2
    )
)
```

## Step 4 — Churn Rate

```dax
Churn Rate =
VAR EligibleBase = [Active Customers] + [Churned Customers]
RETURN
DIVIDE ( [Churned Customers], EligibleBase )
```

Note the denominator deliberately excludes "Never Purchased" and "Not Yet Retained" customers, matching the lesson 1/3 ruling that one-time buyers were never retained and can't churn — including them would understate the real churn rate by inflating the denominator with people who were never at risk of churning in the first place.

## Step 5 — Validate against the SQL output

Before trusting these in a visual, set a slicer to match the SQL query's exact @AsOfDate and region scope, and confirm Churned Customers lands at roughly 1,580 for all regions — matching the T-SQL result from lesson 7. If it doesn't match closely, check for a many-to-many relationship inflating the FILTER's row context before assuming the DAX logic itself is wrong (this exact failure mode is diagnosed in full in lesson 17).

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Built Active Customers as a DISTINCTCOUNT inside a 90-day DATESBETWEEN window, and Churned Customers as a row-context FILTER over VALUES(CustomerID) checking both the inactivity and prior-12-month-purchase conditions per customer, since DAX needs that rebuilt as row logic rather than inheriting SQL's CTE structure. Churn Rate divides churned by (active + churned), deliberately excluding never-purchased and not-yet-retained customers from the denominator.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The core measures are built and validated against the SQL baseline from lesson 7 — within a rounding difference, as expected. These three measures are what both report pages in the next two lessons will be built around.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The dashboard now calculates churn live, the same way it was defined and agreed on — not a one-time number, but something that recalculates correctly as the data updates.

lessons.title: Building the Executive Summary Page
lessons.summary: One page, built for a Sales Director skimming it in under a minute.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: This is the Power BI page the Sales Director actually opens first: three KPI cards, one trend line, and one plain-language callout, built exactly to the wireframe sketched in lesson 6, using the measures built in lesson 9.
lessons.explainSimple: This is where the drawing from the last planning lesson turns into a real screen you can click on. The big numbers go where we sketched them, the line chart goes where we sketched it, and the one-sentence note goes right at the top where it's impossible to miss.
lessons.explainProfessional: This page exists to pass the five-second test from lesson 6, which means resisting the temptation to add "just one more visual." Card visuals for Active Customers, Churned Customers, and Churn Rate sit at the top; conditional formatting on the Churn Rate card provides an at-a-glance severity signal without requiring the reader to know what 4% "should" look like; a line chart gives the trailing-12-month trend so a single snapshot number doesn't get over-interpreted as a change in direction; and a dynamic text box pulls the highest-churn region directly from the model so the callout can't drift out of sync with the data behind it.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Place the three KPI cards

Insert three Card visuals across the top of the page, bound to `[Active Customers]`, `[Churned Customers]`, and `[Churn Rate]`. Format Churn Rate as a percentage with one decimal place.

## Step 2 — Add conditional formatting to the Churn Rate card

Format pane → Callout value → Conditional formatting → Font color, rule-based on the measure value (e.g. green under 3%, amber 3-6%, red above 6%). This lets the Sales Director register severity before reading a single label.

## Step 3 — Add the trailing-12-month trend line

A line chart with `'Date'[Month]` on the axis and `[Churn Rate]` as the value, filtered to the trailing 12 months. This answers "is this new, or has it always been like this" at a glance, which a single point-in-time number cannot.

## Step 4 — Build a dynamic callout, not a static text box

```dax
Top Churn Region Callout =
VAR TopRegion =
    CALCULATETABLE (
        TOPN ( 1, VALUES ( Sales_Customers[Region] ), [Churn Rate], DESC ),
        ALL ( Sales_Customers[Region] )
    )
RETURN
    "Churn is concentrated in " & CONCATENATEX ( TopRegion, Sales_Customers[Region] ) & " — see drill-down."
```

Bind this measure to a Card or a Text box using a dynamic field, so the sentence updates automatically if the underlying numbers shift on refresh, rather than becoming a stale claim someone forgot to edit.

## Step 5 — Resist adding anything else to this page

If there's a visual you're tempted to add that isn't one of the four elements above, it belongs on the drill-down page (lesson 11), not here. Re-run the five-second test from lesson 6 once the page is built, with a different coworker if possible, to confirm it still holds.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Built the exec page to the lesson 6 wireframe: three cards bound to the lesson 9 measures with conditional formatting on Churn Rate, a trailing-12-month trend line, and a DAX-driven dynamic callout using TOPN over Region so the highlighted region can't go stale relative to the data.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The executive summary page is built and matches the agreed layout — no scope additions beyond what was sketched and approved in the planning lesson.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The first thing you'll see when you open the dashboard is the churn rate, how it's trending, and which region is driving it — all in one glance, no digging required.

lessons.title: Building the Drill-Down Page by Region and Segment
lessons.summary: Letting the Southeast follow-up question be answered inside the same report.

lessons.explainSimple: If the executive page is the headline of a news story, this page is the rest of the article. It's for someone who read the headline and now wants to know the details — which region, which group of customers, what the actual numbers are underneath that one big percentage.
lessons.explainProfessional: The matrix visual (Region on rows, Segment on columns, Churn Rate and Churned Customers as values) is the workhorse here, because it lets the reader cross-tabulate two dimensions at once without needing a separate chart for every combination. The bar chart surfaces the ranking visually — which matters because a table of percentages doesn't make "Southeast is roughly double every other region" obvious the way a sorted bar chart does on sight. This directly answers the specific follow-up the Sales Director asked for in lesson 1, one click away, without needing her to manually filter anything herself.

Sum the matrix's Churned Customers column across all regions and confirm it matches the `[Churned Customers]` card on the executive page exactly. If it doesn't, stop — that mismatch is a modeling problem, not a rounding difference, and it's the exact symptom investigated in lesson 17.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Built a Region x Segment matrix and a sorted bar chart off the same lesson 9 measures, with Region/Segment/Loyalty Tier slicers scoped to this page only, plus a bookmark that pre-filters to Southeast as a one-click entry point from the executive page.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The drill-down page is built and directly answers the Southeast follow-up the Sales Director asked for in the very first meeting — she doesn't need a separate request or a separate report for it.
